# Copper December 2010 

- 2010 has been a remarkable year for all commodities prices – both hard and softs – and yet as surprising as this may sound, copper’s anticipated 43% hike in average cash prices this year over 2009 was not even the strongest performance amongst the LME-quoted metals.  Behind copper’s price strength this year has been support from just about every cornerstone available: traditional supply/demand disconnects being met by stock draw downs, the dollar’s relationship to other leading currencies, and new financial trading mechanisms in the form of exchangetraded funds. 

- The key question is of course, where can prices go from here?  Coming in at an expected average of c.$8600/t (US$3.90/lb) for this final quarter of 2010, we should anticipate China’s New Year celebrations as having their usual impact of price suppression either side of the 15-day period from February 3<sup>rd</sup> , a little earlier than in 2010.  Ordinarily, we would expect Q1 prices, therefore, to hold close to the $8600/t mark.  However, with ETF Securities already having got its copper-based ETF off the ground earlier this month – and other such investment vehicles queuing up – we think the pressure on prices will edge to the upside to average $9000/t in Q1 2011 (US$4.08/lb). 

- Spot copper concentrate TC/RCs have stabilised over the past few months in the wake of the five-fold run up in terms between July and October of this year.  According to trade sources, recent spot material on offer from mines in North and South America was sold to merchants at terms ranging from $75/t & 7.5c/lb to $88/t & 8.8c/lb with an overall average of $78/t & 7.8c/lb, i.e. similar to last month’s levels.  Note that these rates apply to very prompt cargos, since the main focus for miners has been to minimise year-end inventories.  In addition, many concentrate sellers still view current spot rates as being a temporary market aberration with the expectation that TC/RCs will fall markedly, potentially after the establishment of a new long-term benchmark or, alternatively in tandem with heightened Chinese buying requirements towards the end of Q1 2011.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market

Developments 

**LME quotes see the year out on a high** 2010 has been a remarkable year for all commodities prices – both hard and softs – and yet as surprising as this may sound, copper’s anticipated 43% hike in average cash prices this year over 2009 was not even the strongest performance amongst the LME-quoted metals.  Nickel has been the star performer this year – up by 47% as a likely average year-on-year, while tin’s 46% increase has attracted a similar level of attention as it did during the famous crisis of 1985-1986 – only this time for all the right reasons (and yes, this is how far back we have to go to find _any_ level of interest in tin!).  While we have often had to cite the financial world as having a more than subtle influence on day-to-day price movements, the common thread between all three top metals’ price performances this year is indeed the classic fundamental of a structural metal deficit – and one which is unlikely to go away for another twelve months at least.  Consequently, these prices continue to push towards fresh highs as we enter 2011.  Meanwhile, at the next tier down are aluminium and zinc, which both show still respectable c.30% year-on-year average cash gains over 2009 despite considerably weaker fundamentals (thereby drawing stronger support from “non-traditional” sources). Finally, the 23% hike in average cash price for lead this year over 2009 would ordinarily be stunning, but the fact that the metal will head into its fourth straight year of surplus in 2011 is arguably the most succinct explanation behind its lowly performance ranking amongst all LME-quoted metals this year. 

**Copper drew upon all supportive measures this year** Behind copper’s price strength this year has been support from just about every cornerstone available: traditional supply/demand disconnects being met by stock draw downs, the dollar’s relationship to other leading currencies, and new financial trading mechanisms in the form of exchange-traded funds.  As we left 2009, we had already endured two to three months of supply disruption, and we felt as early as January – with three strikes ongoing in Chile alone - that this one component in the overall picture would underpin a good measure of price support for the coming year.  Factoring in a mere 1.4% supply-side increase this year over 2009 back then, we felt justified in targeting a 38% average cash price hike to $7100/t (US$3.22/lb) in our January report.  Despite strike action at leading operations and other disruptions, supply has in fact done better than we thought.  But the likely 3.8% increase here has been overtaken by the double-digit surge in demand across all principal consuming nations, and so the response from metal producers has been woefully inadequate after all.  At the start of the year, coming out of a poor 18 months or so of metals demand across the board, we considered our forecast global demand increase of c.6% for 2010 to be pretty aggressive.  But, like most ma

rket watchers, we underestimated the extent of the de-stocking that had taken place during that bleak period, and, during March and April this year especially, buyers just could not afford to hold off any longer even in the face of rising metal prices and had to return to the market to replenish supplies. **Stock changes not convincing at first** While the strength in demand was clearly evident in rapidly diminishing stocks on the LME and from Comex warehouses from as early as March, stocks reported by China’s SHFE actually rose for the first four months of the year, and begged the question of whether metal was merely being transferred from one location to another. Then suddenly, on April 14th , when the market tried for a second time to rally copper prices past the $8000/t mark and failed, interest in the red metal evaporated. Buying – whether for stock replenishment or new orders – not surprisingly fell away in the declining price environment, and prices headed into the traditional northern hemisphere summer mode a full month early, touching a low of just $6091/t (US$2.76/lb) on June 8th . From then on, however, copper’s price outlook picked up a notch – but the spark did not come from within the metal’s own fundamentals themselves. #### **Copper price and $US trade-weighted index** 9500

**Dollar:euro exchange rate story kicks in** It was around early June that the relationship between the metaldenominated currency of the US dollar came under scrutiny against other currencies, namely the euro. Opening the year at US$1.43:€1, the dollar strengthened to average US$1.22:€1 during June. But then this trend reversed, and consecutive monthly average declines since July look likely to leave the dollar at year’s end at a similar level to where it kicked off in January. The impact on copper since mid-year has been supportive, and came at a time when the metal’s own fundamentals alone were looking for _any_ direction. The currency change got copper over the lowest price points of the year and into the third quarter, and allowed the fresh metal orders that usually come at that ti

me of year to make their mark on prices yet again. Since June’s average low for the year on a monthly basis of $6500/t (US$2.95/lb), cash copper has breached new targets virtually every month, culminating in maintaining a sustained level in December of beyond $9000/t (US$4.08/lb), and indeed setting a record high of $9260/t (US$4.20/lb) on the 14th of this month. **Exchange-traded fund mechanism to play a role in metals pricing going forward** Midway between that July turnaround and the current highs, and right at the time of the main international metals trading gathering that is LME Week, emerged a second “non-traditional” and bullish influence on metals prices, with copper and aluminium benefiting in particular. Two companies - JP Morgan and Blackrock Asset Management - filed applications with the US SEC to set up exchange-traded funds (ETFs). With one of the key criteria for a physical metal ETF to succeed being higher prices, it shows that there is a widespread opinion within the financial community that higher copper prices will indeed prevail. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 800 Refined Imports 400

There are regional issues that will conspire to firm up the market next year, too. In North America, the closure of two refineries, plus lower output from two others, will keep the pressure on prices and premia, and Comex stocks, having declined from over 95kt (metric) in mid-January to sub-60kt today, will do little to offset any tightness. In Europe, Russia’s new export tax on cathode will restrict supplies and push semi processed rod into the region instead. In Asia, that Codelco has set near record premia on its cathode sales underlines what the world’s largest producer thinks of the strength of the market ahead. **Even the unknown quantity of Chinese stocks are not presenting concern to the market** The only fly in the ointment in our view to this scenario is the level of unreported stocks held off exchange in the Chinese market. They are not to be ignored, but if they are indeed at the lower of the rumoured range of between 200-500kt, then even this can easily be mopped up if Chinese demand tests our 7% year-on-year growth forecast. Meanwhile, total LME stocks have also fallen by 21% since the start of the year, and have been falling on a consistent basis through the year, suggesting that there has been sufficient ongoing demand strength even through to the end of the year. **Low stock days to underpin higher price forecasts for the next two years** Having increased by more than 40% year-on-year, the question is where prices can go from here? Coming in at an expected average of c.$8600/t (US$3.90/lb) for this final quarter of 2010, we should anticipate China’s New Year celebrations as having their usual impact of price suppression either side of the 15-day period from February 3rd , a little earlier than in 2010. Ordinarily, we would expect Q1 prices, therefore, to ho

ld close to the $8600/t mark.  However, with ETF Securities already having got its copper-based ETF off the ground earlier this month – and other such investment vehicles queuing up – we think the pressure on prices will edge to the upside to average $9000/t in Q1 2011 (US$4.08/lb).  By the second quarter, we expect to see Chinese buyers ringing in the “Year of the Hare” by returning to the market with apposite haste, and this will test producers’ ability to keep pace with strong offtake.  In our view, it will be this mismatch and the resultant effect on stock days of consumption that will turn up the heat on prices another notch.  We expect to see _daily_ price closings of $10,000/t (US$4.54/lb – cash) during the second quarter, and monthly _averages_ at this level by Q3 and into Q4 as stock days fall initially below the 60-day level by late-Q2, and then into the mid-40s range by mid-Q3.  Consequently, we forecast 2011’s average cash copper price reaching $9700/t (US$4.40/lb), and only minor pressure release coming by H2 2012 will bring average prices down for that year to $9100/t (US$4.13/lb).  In short, it would be difficult to make a case for any weakness in copper prices for the next two years.  For now, at least, the _promise_ of fresh metal from largescale projects in the medium term that should be the trigger-point for price relief remains nothing more than that.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

**Surprising demand strength during 2010…** After a flat 2008 (+0.2% year-on-year growth in global copper demand) and then the most severe drop-off in 2009 (-2.7% y-o-y) since 1982 (down by 5.5% y-o-y), we came into 2010 with what we believed to be a bold near 6% y-o-y increase in global demand, as per our January report.  In the event, the extent of the refined metal and semis stock draw downs during 2009 set the stage for a stronger comeback across all metals than most if not all analysts predicted 12 months ago, and copper has been no exception.  Having begun the year with a 5.9% forecast increase in demand for 2010, which would have taken the global primary figure up to 18.478Mt – a new record, even then – our current estimate of copper demand for this year now stands at 19.3Mt and represents a 10.4% y-o-y surge which is 1.3Mt up on the prior high set in 2008. 

**..and demand growth still evident in 2011** Furthermore, we believe we can expect solid demand growth into next year, even if in percentage terms it does not appear as immediately attractive at “just” 4.5%.  This year’s strength has been the result of two major components: a need to replenish the stock draw downs, and a response to fresh, ongoing demand.  Next year, we doubt that the stock replenishment element will be as strong, and the high metal prices we have seen this year (and expect to see going forward) have brought out much more scrap from dealers who have held onto it for some time but are now

prepared to release it.  In addition, some of the new demand that we have seen this year has been the result of government-sponsored incentive schemes and tax breaks that will no longer be in place in most Western World developed nations into 2011.  There can be no doubt that these schemes have made a strong contribution to the 8.2% y-o-y demand growth in copper this year, and equally their absence will be sorely noticed next year, which partly explains why we have only 1.2% copper demand growth for the Western World in 2011.  China continues to run with several such schemes, however, and they will be an important driver behind our 7% y-o-y growth profile in 2011. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**European copper demand surges in 2010** Such was the doom and gloom in Europe during the latter stages of 2008 and throughout 2009 that it was difficult to find any hopeful cause coming into 2010.  But this was the region where arguably most of the de-stocking of all copper products has been taking place.  Consequently, our current estimate of 12.2% y-o-y demand growth for Western Europe’s mature economies still calls for a double-take even now.  But before we get too excited about that percentage figure, though, it is worth bearing in mind that the 3.072Mt demand rate for this year is almost 0.97Mt lower than the regional record set in 2000, and 0.85Mt down on the more recent “recovery” year of 2006.  Consequently, we believe that the over-riding trend in regional copper demand is edging lower due to the hollowing-out effect at the manufacturing level, and year-on-year surges in demand figures like the double-digit change that we have seen this year are more than likely to be the result of refined metal and product stock changes than any reversal of that underlying bearish demand trend. 

**Much lower expectations for next year** Going into 2011, we are showing no improvement at all in overall regional copper demand.  As with this year, though, there will be individual countries where demand will shine.  Germany, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Belgium have all done better this year than we were initially expecting, and the financial results from Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, demonstrate that.  This month it posted a 33% improvement in gross profit for its 2009-2010 fiscal year (ending Sept 30<sup>th</sup> ) as a result of the better than expected markets.  Citing high utilisation rates across its copper-refining and semis-manufacturing facilities, Aurubis reported strong demand for copper products, especially wire rod, benefitting from the stronger auto and energy sectors this year. 

Ample scrap availability offset slightly lower concentrates throughput to push cathode output at the three main sites of Hamburg, Olen and Pirdop that comprise its Primary Copper Business Unit up by 4.6% to 932kt _vs._ the prior fiscal year’s 889kt.  Meanwhile, at its Recycling and Precious Metals Business Unit cathode production from the Lunen, Germany facility

increased by 7.5% to 212kt for the Oct 2009-Sept 2010 period. This improvement in availability of cathode allowed an equally strong performance from the company’s Copper Products business Unit, with a 23% hike in wire rod output (to 766kt) and a 37% increase in continuous cast shapes produced (210kt vs. 153kt). Aurubis expects continued high capacity utilisation rates across its plants going into 2011, despite lower national economic performances due to tighter spending controls. There was also an accident at the Hamburg smelter in early December which will keep that equipment offline for at least two weeks and will therefore reduce anode availability to its associated refinery. But Aurubis has not yet said what overall impact on production this incident will have as it will attempt to address any immediate shortfall by inter-group product redirection. **European economic development is the main concern** This issue of lower spending expected for next year will no doubt be the main impediment to any improvement in regional copper demand. As we noted last month, the fact that Eire became the second country of the region to accept a financial bail-out recently from the IMF/EU means that there is considerable uncertainty going forward. This month we note that Moody’s is putting Spain’s A1A credit rating under review, lending credence to the ever-widening belief that Eire and Greece will not be the only EU member states to hold their arms aloft. Spain’s economy has suffered due to the impoverished construction and auto sectors, and copper demand has trended lower as a result. This year’s uplift to c.285kt was due to re-stocking requirements, and we expect a return to the recent annual averages of c.260kt in 2011. **Russia and Romania changing their demand profiles this year and next** Earlier this year we noted that Romania’s sole copper wire rod facility at Zalau had closed. Since then, it has been importing all of its c.30-40kt annualised of rod in order to keep its wire-making lines busy, and this squares with reports that we have heard of strong rod demand from the Former East Europe region. Company owner Cuprom has turned to imports of rod to keep its Baie Mare wire-making equipment gainfully employed, with rod makers in Italy, Germany, Greece and Belgium proving to be the main beneficiaries. Consequently, we have reduced our Romanian primary copper consumption forecast for this year from 12kt to 4kt. Meanwhile, Russia first use copper consumption is expected to surge in 2011 after a change in the tax regime from the middle o

f this month will likely entice much of the cathode that was formerly exported to stay at home for processing by domestic facilities. Consequently, Europe can expect to see some tightness in cathode supplies going into 2011, and premia could easily edge up as a result. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2010 Page 7 of 23 Copper Monthly Update ### **Americas** **US copper demand proving resilient** In the USA, we have made significant increases throughout the year for both 2009 and 2010 copper demand. Again, as per Europe, there was more than expected de-stocking of all copper products after the economic fall-out of late-2008, and these stocks needed considerable pipeline replenishment. Our 2009 estimate has been upgraded from the 1.55Mt shown at the start of this year to 1.65Mt currently, while this year’s forecast also went up from 1.56Mt to 1.75Mt. We expect this level to hold into 2011. **Copper rod output remains strong…** Production of copper wire rod for September of 108kt has maintained the average output rate at 10% higher than the first nine months of last year, according to data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics. With strong exports in September and static import business, this left apparent consumption of wire rod for the first nine months of the year up by 5.9% at c.950kt. Despite the poor construction sector, strong performances from autos, which are on target for a c.15% year on year increase in output, will have contributed to the robust rod production. Domestic rod shipments slipped slightly in September (by a negligible 1.7kt), but were up by 83.1kt (9.6%) over the nine-month period in 2009 to 952.3kt. Even so, the market was not strong enough for all participants to survive, with Sherburne Metal Products closing its small, 15kt/a capacity rod mill in NY state during the third quarter, and its future is as uncertain as were the circumstances over its closure. #### **US copper wire rod production – (kt)** 40 125

**..but tube sector continues to suffer due to poor construction rates** If the US wire rod sector seems to be holding up reasonably well this year, the same cannot be said for the tube business, reflecting th

e poor construction market. Negative equity from housing fallout will continue to be the main drag. According to latest American Bureau of Metal Statistics data, apparent consumption of copper tube reached c.871kt (metric) for the first nine months of this year. This is up by only a modest 1.2% on Jan-Sept 2009 data, but Q3 figures did show the first year-on-year quarterly increase since Q2 2006. Even so, domestic shipments remained depressed, down by 6.5% at 209kt, and this low level of business has continued to pose problems for even some of the bigger players. On November 1st , Huntsville, Alabamabased Wolverine Tube Inc filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in order to restructure its $100M of debt. Given that it has the support of its noteholders, Wolverine hopes to emerge from bankruptcy within 90 days with c.$30M of debt but at more favourable repayment terms and to continue operating in the interim. Wolverine’s move comes almost a year after another player in the fragmented tube business – Cambridge-Lee Industries, and its Mexican parent Cobre de Pasteje – both filed for Chapter 11 proceedings in December 2009. In the wire sector, too, there has been a fair amount of consolidation this year. Carrollton, GA-based Southwire built on its Q1 acquisition of American Insulated Wire Corp by adding Tappan Wire and Cable to its stable in July. Blauvelt, NYbased Tappan supplies the electronics, signal/control, industrial, HVAC and OEM markets with a wide range of cable products covering security and access control, coaxial video, fire alarm and custom electronics cables. This was Southwire’s second major acquisition of this year, having bought all the assets of American Insulated Wire in late February. AIW has factories in Douglas, GA and Coffeyville, KS making building wire products for commercial and industrial sectors and OEMs. AIW had been a subsidiary of Melville, NY-based electrical and electronic products manufacturer, Leviton, since 1936. **Improvement in copper consumption met by stock** Again, according to the ABMS, apparent consumption of refined copper increased by 3.8% during the third quarter vs. Q2, and was up by almost 19% on year ago levels. September’s Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2010 Page 8 of 23 Copper Monthly Update consumption rate of 155.6kst was 20.5% up on the same month of 2009. However, with domestic cathode shipments and net imports both down this year by 2.5% and 10.3% to 923kst and 411.6kst, respectively, the increase in copper consumption has clearly been met by draw downs in stock. The ABMS calculates that the 38kst of stock draw downs from the range of producers, consumers and LME/Comex warehouses accounted for c.3% of US apparent refined copper consumption so far this year. #### **US brass mill shipments – (kt)** 20 100

### **China** **Economy in good shape for 2011 despite managed slowdown** Chinese industrial production growth has slowed through the second half of 2010, in line with expectations. Output in November was still up by an impressive 13.3% year on year though, while the slowdown is as much a factor of a higher base effect from 2009 as the result of tighter monetary policy and restrictions in the real estate sector. However, following the latest 50 basis point hike in bank reserve requirements, allied to hawkish comments from officials, further slowdown is expected. That said, given the positive near term leading indicators, such as the industrial PMI up to 55.2 in November, we expect any slowdown to come in Q2, suggesting solid momentum behind underlying copper demand in the first quarter, despite the obvious disruption from the Chinese New Year. **Fog to be lifted on apparent consumption?** Last month we touched on the perceived slump in demand that was apparent from a dip in refined output but a much sharper fall in imports. At the time we pointed out that the Golden Week holidays were most likely the culprit behind the slip rather than a sharp fall off in demand and November’s preliminary imports data of 351.6kt confirmed this, putting imports back on the weighted average track for a 2010. However, even with the return to form of imports, apparent consumption might be overcooking demand to some degree given that at least a portion of recent imports have been going into bonded warehouses. The recent proposal by SHFE to allow this material to be delivered against contracts supports this view and although approval is still required by the China Securities and Regulatory Commission, it is expected that the facility will be available from the first quarter of 2011. The impact on demand would be to shift stocks from unreported to reported in SHFE’s warehouses and thus help to remove the fog at least over part of the demand picture in China. **Consumer appetite remains strong…** With real interest rates negative, this ought to encourage big-ticket purchases and indeed, consumer goods sales increased by 18.7% year on year in November. Significantly, any tightening in credit availability is unlikely to crimp consumer demand directly in China given that most purchases are made from savings rather than loans and this should, therefore, provide further impetus to consumer durables production. **…although construction’s foundations are less firm** Despite all the policy tightening aimed at real estate, construction activity across China continues to boom for the time being, spurred on by government initiatives to increase the supply of low-cost housing. However, there has been an increasing divergence between construction starts versus completions and sales in 2010, indicating the possibility of a large overhang of

near-completed inventory. A sharper drop in construction volumes in 2011 than we are forecasting would have severe implications for China’s industrial growth, in addition to affecting copper semis demand. ## Concentrate Markets 

**Spot concentrate buying terms remain stable in December** Spot copper concentrate TC/RCs have stabilised over the past few months in the wake of the five-fold run up in terms between July and October of this year.  According to trade sources, recent spot material on offer from mines in North and South America were sold to merchants at terms ranging from $75/t & 7.5c/lb to $88/t & 8.8c/lb with an overall average of $78/t & 7.8c/lb, i.e. similar to last month’s levels. Note that these rates apply to very prompt cargos, since the main focus for miners has been to minimise year-end inventories.  In addition, many concentrate sellers still view current spot rates as being a temporary market aberration with the expectation that TC/RCs will fall markedly, potentially after the establishment of a new long-term benchmark or, alternatively in tandem with heightened Chinese buying requirements towards the end of Q1 2011.  Concentrate inventories at most Chinese smelters remain at comfortable levels which has continued to dampen fresh buying interest. The last spot trade heard in this market was transacted at $90/t & 9.0c/lb, which is a little lower than what was being reported last month ($93/t & 9.3c/lb).  The Indian market has not been particularly active of late either.  The country’s Supreme Court has adjourned to the third week of January a hearing on an appeal filed by Sterlite Industries to keep its copper smelter running following a High Court decision to close the smelter after hearing petitions challenging the plant’s environmental clearance.

**China’s demand for imported concentrates to continue rising in 2011** China’s demand for imported concentrates looks set to increase further in 2011 on the basis of smelter developments that have occurred in 2010 and that are expected in 2011.  This year has seen the commissioning of the 60kt/a Hengbang smelter in Shandong province in May, the 100kt/a Kunpeng’s Liangshan plant in Sichuan at the end of August, the 100kt/a Chifeng Fubang smelter in Inner Mongolia in October, Tianzhong’s 100kt/a IsaSmelt plant in Yunnan and Daye’s new 400kt/a Ausmelt operation at the start of December.  In addition, Huludao’s 150kt/a Ausmelt project has been completed and is due to be fully commissioned in 2011, as is Yunnan Tin’s 100kt/a Ausmelt plant in Yunnan and Zijin Mining’s 200kt/a flash smelter in Fujian province (probably in July).  Elsewhere, Shandong Xiangguang is due to complete an expansion to double the capacity of its flash smelting and converting complex to 400kt/a by April 2011 and Yunnan Copper aims to restart its 200kt/a IsaSmelt operation at around the same time.  The Yunnan plant has been closed since mid-2010 for extended maintenance.  Offsetting these gains are/will be various closures involving smelters that utilise antiquated technology. Tianzhong’s new smelter has replaced the 40kt/a Chuxiong reverberatory furnace, while Yunnan Tin’s 100kt/a plant will replace the 40kt/a Gejiu reverb.  Elsewhere, Zhongtiaoshan closed its 50kt/a Yuanqu reverb and is constructing a new 100kt/a furnace that will be commissioned in 2012.  Similarly, Daye’s 50kt/a reverb will be phased out in tandem with the start up of the Ausmelt plant.  Overall, over the period 2010 to 2011 the net growth in China’s primary copper smelting industry will be 1.14Mt, comprising 1.31Mt of brownfield and greenfield capacity additions and 180kt of closures. 

**Chinese primary smelter output in 2011 to be constrained by concentrate availability** China’s smelter output in 2011 is likely to be constrained by the availability of concentrates.  As the table below shows, domestic copper-inconcentrates production is expected to increase by 70kt next year with concentrate imports rising by 6.6%, or 110kt Cu for a total uplift in primary feed of 180kt Cu.  For 2012 the projected additions to China’s primary smelter feed are estimated to be 390kt Cu, comprising 70kt from domestic sources and 320kt from imports.  Note that despite the forecast rise in China’s smelter and refinery production (+1Mt between 2010 and 2

012) the country’s net cathode import requirements are not expected to fall over the next few years due to the country’s ongoing strong metal demand growth.

However, perhaps more importantly, another factor is the upcoming change in VAT rebate policy for the Chinese secondary industry. For many years, the Chinese government had been supporting the country’s recycling industry through permitting a VAT exemption on this sector. However, at the end of 2008 this policy was amended with the introduction of a VAT rate of 10% but with a 70% rebate applicable in 2009 that was reduced to 50% in 2010. Commencing from the start of 2011 the rebate is to be removed altogether. This will affect scrap yards, secondary smelters and refineries as well as semis producers. In anticipation of this change in policy, a number of scrap consumers have been stockpiling material ahead of the year-end deadline in order to qualify for the rebate. Any new deals with scrap suppliers will clearly miss the rebate deadline and the combination of this and the acceleration in purchases ahead of the deadline (November’s imports increased by over 30% year on year to a provisional 400kt) has contributed to slower uptake this month. As a consequence, US No.2 scrap spreads have widened even further over the past few weeks, from 55c/lb under March Comex to 65c/lb below at present. **No blister tenders of note in December** There have been no tenders of note thus far in December. **Rio Tinto and Ivanhoe sign new agreement for the development of Oyu Tolgoi** Rio Tinto and Ivanhoe Mines have signed a new agreement under which Rio Tinto will assume direct management of the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold project in Mongolia.  Rio will also provide a comprehensive financial package to Ivanhoe Mines that is expected to help secure the development of the project approximately six months ahead of schedule in late 2012.  Rio will deliver a $1.8Bn interim loan facility while the two companies complete project financing.  The company will also secure the right to increase its ownership in Ivanhoe to 49%.  Rio Tinto has also agreed to suspend its arbitration in relation to the Shareholders Rights Plan by six months to June 2011 and to extend the standstill arrangement by three months to January 2012.  Phase I capital costs are forecast to be $4.5Bn with $2.3Bn due to be spent in 2011 and a further $2Bn in 2012.  Construction work at Oyu Tolgoi is progressing ahead of schedule with first production now forecast to commence in late 2012.  Initial ore throughput will be sourced from the Southern Oyu open pit at a rate of 100kt/d and by 2017 ore mining rates will be raised to 160kt/d with the commissioning of the Hugo North underground mine.  Average annual production during the first ten years of operations is projected to be 544kt/a of copper-in-concentrates and 650koz of gold.

**CST pulls first cathodes at Lady Annie** CST Mining (formerly China Sci-Tech Holdings) re

ports that it has harvested the first batch of cathodes from its recently-acquired Lady Annie SxEw mine which is located 120km northwest of Mt Isa in Queensland.  The mine was previously owned by CopperCo which went into receivership in November 2008.  Cape Lambert then acquired the property after it took over CopperCo in May 2009.  CST Mining paid Cape Lambert $132M for Lady Annie, which has proven and probable reserves of 11.2Mt grading 1.1% Cu.  The capacity of the operation is 30kt/a Cu although CST expects to produce 20-25kt in 2011.

**Muliashi development hampered by rain** Construction progress at the Muliashi SxEw project in Zambia has been hampered by heavy rains.  Bad weather conditions are also delaying the delivery of materials and equipment from overseas.  China Nonferrous Metal Corp.  acquired the project after winning a government auction to buy Luanshya Copper Mines.  The overall capital cost is put at $350M and start up is earmarked for 2013.  At capacity Muliashi should be capable of producing 60kt/a of SxEw copper as well as 1.5kt/a of cobalt. 

**Metorex resumes full output at Ruashi** Metorex has now resumed full production at its Ruashi copper mine in the DRC.  Output had been constrained by a recurring electrical problem in the SxEw tank house that, according to the company, is likely to result in a 20% drop in production in Q4 relative to the 8.6kt produced in Q3.  Cobalt production is also expected to drop, by 16% from the Q3 figure of 1.1kt. 

**Bor secures financing for smelter upgrade** RTB Bor has entered into a $170M loan agreement with the Canadian Agency for Export and Development that will be provided to the Serbian copper producer in a combination of euros and US dollars.  The funds will be employed to modernise the company’s antiquated copper smelter by replacing the reverberatory furnaces and ancillary equipment with modern flash smelting technology and an acid plant upgrade.  SNC Lavalin will be the main contractor with the smelter equipment supplied by Outotec.  The new smelter will have a rated capacity of 400kt/a of concentrates which is equivalent to approximately 80kt/a of copper.  Most of the feed for the new smelter will be sourced from Bor’s own mines that are also in the throes of being upgraded and modernised.  Current copper production varies between 30-40kt/a using one of the two reverberatory lines in the existing smelter.  The loan repayment period is ten years with a grace period of three years.
